en: The Ritual Manual for the Yoga Contemplation of the Heart Mantra of the Holy Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
extracted from the Mahāvairocana-abhisaṃbodhi Sūtra. Compiled by [Name],
Grand Master of the Household, Peer of the State, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Duke of Sui.

The Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery—who was granted a fief of three thousand households, invested with the purple robe, posthumously honored as Minister of Works, and bestowed with the title of Great Mirror and the posthumous name of Righteousness—translated this by imperial decree. Now, as for those who practice Yoga:
First, establish a maṇḍala in a quiet place.
Sprinkle it with scented water and scatter various seasonal flowers upon the altar.
The practitioner must first bathe and don fresh, clean robes.
Next, entering the ritual arena before the honored image,
they should prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground, generating a heart of profound sincerity.
Homage to all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas. Then,
assuming the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*),
one should visualize all Buddhas as if they were present before one's eyes.
Thereafter, with utmost sincerity, one should repent of all transgressions,
speaking these words:
"I, [Name], from time immemorial until now..."
From beginningless saṃsāra until this very day,
we have committed immeasurable and boundless transgressions— whether committed by ourselves,
incited in others, or rejoiced in seeing others commit them— without being aware of them.
I now repent and shall not create [such karma] again.
I only pray that all Buddhas will compassionately accept me, so that my karmic obstacles may be swiftly extinguished. (Recite this three times.)
Furthermore, one should personally vow to receive the precepts of the Three Refuges,
speaking these words:
"May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas compassionately protect me."
I, [Name], from this day forth until I sit at the seat of enlightenment,
take refuge in the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed three bodies.
I take refuge in the Mahāyāna Dharma-treasury;
I take refuge in the Saṃgha of all Bodhisattvas. (Recite this three times.
I, [Name], have completed taking refuge in the Buddha, have completed taking refuge in the Dharma, and have completed taking refuge in the Saṃgha.
From this day forth until the attainment of Buddhahood,
I shall never again turn to other vehicles or external paths;
I only pray that all Buddhas will compassionately accept me.
Next, one should offer one's body as an offering.
One should speak these words:
"May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, out of compassion, take pity on me."
May you accept me.
From this day forth until I attain Buddhahood,
I shall constantly sacrifice my body to make offerings to all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas.
"May you, out of compassion and pity, grant your protection"— thus he says three times. Next,
in the space at the very bottom,
he visualizes the syllable *Ha*, which is black in color.
That syllable transforms into a wind-wheel,
crescent-shaped; upon this wind-wheel, [it rests].
One should visualize the syllable VAṂ as white in color;
that syllable transforms into a water-maṇḍala, perfectly circular in shape.
Upon this water-maṇḍala...
One should visualize the syllable RA as golden in color.
This syllable transforms into a fierce vajra from which issue vajra flames in a triangular shape.
From the bottom upward, reaching as far as the earth-wheel and one's own body,
the flames burn them until only ashes remain;
these very ashes then transform into a vajra-wheel.
Its wheel is white in color and firm and dense;
according to its size, it is square in shape.
It is situated upon the vajra-wheel.
Visualize a great eight-petaled lotus flower,
complete with jeweled filaments and anthers;
upon the center of this lotus pedestal, [place the object of meditation].
Visualize the syllable *Sva* above, golden in color;
this syllable possesses immeasurable light and transforms into the Noble Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Seated in the full lotus posture, his body was like the color of gold;
a radiant halo blazed intensely around him,
and he wore light gauze and brocade garments with a crimson skirt.
The left hand is held at the navel grasping an unopened lotus flower;
the right hand is placed at the chest in the gesture of opening the petals of a flower.
He is adorned with a crown and necklaces.
With the image of Amitāyus Buddha upon his head, he dwells in the state of meditative concentration.
Having performed this visualization,
he immediately binds the Samaya-mudrā.
Place both hands at the heart,
join the palms closely together, and extend the two thumbs upward.
Recite the mantra as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām āḥ samaya-cittamaya svāhā.* Recite this mantra three times.
One empowers the five places by sealing them with the mudrā;
that is to say, one seals the forehead, the right shoulder, the left shoulder, the heart, and the crown of the head, dispersing [the mudrā] from there.
By forming this mudrā, [one is empowered].
One is then able to swiftly fulfill the practices and vows of the ten stages and the ten pāramitās;
one is able to perceive the stage of all Tathāgatas and is able to transcend the realm of the path of dharmas.

That which is called "surpassing the stage of resolute conviction" (*adhimukti-bhūmi*), the "stage of the pure mind" (*śuddhi-citta-bhūmi*), and the "stage of the Tathāgata" (*tathāgata-bhūmi*) is the "surpassing of the realm of the path of phenomena" (*dharma-mārga-dhātu*).
Next, bind the *dharmadhātu-sambhava-mudrā*:
with both hands, form vajra-fists and place them side by side.
Extend both index fingers with their tips touching side by side and place them upon the crown of the head; then,
visualize the syllable *raṃ* at the crown of the head.
White light flows forth from the syllable,
illuminating one's own body as well as the internal and external environments;
one then contemplates that one's own body is identical to the dharmadhātu.
Recite the mantra:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ dharmadhātu-svabhāvātmaka*. Recite this mantra three times.
Separate the mudrā from the crown of the head;
let the two fists gradually open and disperse to both sides.
Next, form the Dharma-Wheel-Turning Mudrā.
Place both hands at the heart with the backs touching,
the right hand pressing down upon the left,
and the four fingers interlaced.
The left thumb is hidden within the right palm;
the tips of the thumbs of both hands are pressed together.
Visualize yourself as the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva.
With your left hand, hold a vajra bell and place it upon your left hip;
with your right hand, hold a five-pronged vajra at your heart in a leaping posture.
One’s body is like the color of the moon, wearing a crown of the five buddhas and seated upon a lunar disc.
Recite the mantra: *Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ vajratma ko haṃ*. Having recited this mantra three times—
Immediately, one performs the mudrā of scattering upon the crown of the head.
Next, one binds the sword-mudrā of Vairocana Tathāgata:
with both hands joined in *añjali* at the heart.
Bend the middle joints of the two index fingers and place them horizontally against each other. With the two thumbs,
press down together upon the upper joints of the two index fingers, forming the shape of a sword.
Having bound this mudrā,
one should immediately visualize an eight-petaled lotus within one's own heart.
Within that lotus, one should imagine the syllable ĀḤ.
Emitting golden light in conjunction with the mudrā,
one should contemplate that the syllable *Āḥ* realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
Then, recite the mantra as follows:
Recite the mantra *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ vīra hūṃ khaṃ* eight times.
With the mudrā as before, consecrate five places on one's own body.
Disperse the mudrā over the crown of the head.
Next, bind the mudrā of universal offering:
join the two hands in *añjali*.
Press the right hand over the left, crossing the fingers at the first joints, and the seal is formed.
Recite the mantra: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ sarvathā udgate sphara hīṃ gagana-khaṃ svāhā*. Bind the seal at the heart.
Recite the mantra five times.
Visualize that from the mudrā, immeasurable and boundless incense, flowers, food, and drink flow forth,
making offerings to all the worthy and holy ones throughout the entirety of space and the whole dharma-realm.
One should perform the mudrā-dissolution at the crown of the head;
next, the practitioner of yoga should visualize the method for the sequential arrangement of syllables.
Place the syllable HŪṂ between one's own eyebrows;
it is reddish-gold in color and transforms into the mark of the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa).
Place the syllable *Aṃ* within the junction of the brain;
white light fills the interior of the brain.
Place the syllable *Rāṃ* upon the crown of the head.
Visualize red-colored light rays with upward-flaming tips surging forth from the crown of the Buddha’s head;
at the crown of his head, one should imagine a white syllable Oṃ emitting light that illuminates the entire Dharma-realm.
Then, place the syllable Svā on the sole of one’s own right foot.
Place the syllable *Ha* upon the sole of the left foot.
Then, contemplate one's own mind as the bodhicitta,
free from all notions of self and free from the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), as well as from subject and object.
Regarding the equality of all phenomena,
one should understand that one's own mind is primordially unborn, empty, and devoid of intrinsic nature;
therefore, one should investigate it in this way.
One's own mind does not possess the nature of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Why is this? Because those natures of a self, a person, and so forth—
Because there is nothing created and nothing attained, the self,
persons, and so forth are fundamentally non-existent;
how could they possess intrinsic nature?
One immediately attains the distancing from all views of a self.
Furthermore, this mind is not of the nature of the aggregates, bases, or elements. Why is this?

Because this nature of the aggregates and so forth cannot be found in reality within the ultimate sense, the intrinsic nature of the distinctions among the aggregates, bases, and elements [is non-existent].
It is not that mind; this mind is neither the grasper nor the grasped,
nor is it that mind of deluded conceptualization which acts as the grasper.
Because it does not take up such characteristics as blue or yellow,
the Blessed One said:
"The mind does not abide within, nor does it abide without, nor does it abide in between."
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally pure and free from conceptual discrimination.
Observing in this way, one knows that one’s own mind is selfless and equal.
One thoroughly understands that all phenomena are originally unarisen,
free from false conceptualization,
and entirely devoid of intrinsic nature, like empty space.
Contemplating all sentient beings with compassion,
[he saw that] since beginningless time they have not known that their own minds are originally pure;
thus they give rise to false discrimination, being devoured by the demons of perversion.
"Enduring various sufferings within saṃsāra,
how shall I now arouse great diligence so that all sentient beings may awaken to their own minds?"
Having realized the dharma of complete purity,
it causes others to distance themselves from false conceptualization;
such great compassion constitutes the bodhicitta.
Having generated this mind,
one places a circular dot (bindu) above the syllable RA;
it thus becomes the syllable RAṂ, which is the seed-syllable of the Dharmadhātu.
Visualize two syllables *raṃ* placed within the two eyes,
like lamps filled with light that universally illumines all things.
By means of this light, one employs the eye of wisdom.
Contemplate the letter *Ā* placed within one's own mind;
realize that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen,
and from that letter *Ā*, white light radiates forth.
It illuminates world-systems as numerous as the sands of the boundless Ganges,
removing the darkness of ignorance and delusion within the bodies of all sentient beings.
Then, one should visualize oneself transforming into Vairocana Tathāgata.
Wearing a crown and necklaces, seated upon a white lotus flower,
his body golden in color and radiant with light, he dwells in samādhi;
one should contemplate him in accordance with this visualization.
Next, bind the heart-seal of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:
interlace the two hands with the palms facing inward and extend both thumbs upward.
The mudrā is thus formed.
Place the seal at the heart and recite the Heart Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva seven times.
Empower the heart, forehead, throat, and crown with the mudrā, reciting the mantra:
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ kākāsana svāhā. Recite this mantra accordingly.
With the right thumb, beckon [the deity] toward oneself.
This constitutes the invocation. Then, visualize that upon the heart of the principal deity is a perfectly tranquil moon disc.
Within this moon disc, the syllables of the dhāraṇī are arranged in a clockwise direction.
All those syllables emit white light that pervades the entire dharma-realm;
this light returns and enters the crown of the practitioner’s head,
into the moon-disc within the heart of the one practicing yoga.
Arrange them clearly and distinctly, rotating to the right as before.
Furthermore, let those characters emit light.
Perform the visualization as before.
Having observed in this way,
the practitioner of yoga perceives their own body as being equal to and indistinguishable from the body of the deity Avalokiteśvara.
Just as those mirror-images are neither identical nor different, one should next contemplate the meaning of the syllables.
Regarding the gateway of the letter A (Ā): it is because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
The letter-gateway *ra* signifies that all phenomena are free from dust.
The letter-gateway *la* signifies that the characteristics of all phenomena are unattainable;
this letter *la* is used here as an augmentative sound.
It transforms into the syllable *bala*.
From within this syllable *bala*,
the syllable *ka* flows forth.
The gateway of the letter KA is because all phenomena are without fabrication;
one should contemplate in this way, fixing the mind upon the syllables of the mantra and then reflecting on the meanings signified by those letters.
That is to say, one performs the visualization on the four meanings above, such as "primordial non-arising," ending and then beginning again;
this is called *samādhi* recitation. If one performs recitation with audible voice, [it is called verbal recitation].
Within the mantra, one should insert this phrase.
Recite the mantra as follows:
Oṃ āluṅkari cire ḍiṅkiśami vibhūtiṃ nana svāhā. Next, one should visualize the four syllables beginning with *ā* and *luṅka* as being golden in color.
By reciting the aforementioned mantra, one immediately attains increase;
whatever is sought within the Dharma shall be obtained.
As previously visualized, there is the letter Ā in the heart and the letter AṂ in the brain.
Their essence is one.
Within the eye is the syllable RA, and upon its crown is the syllable RAṂ;
such is the meaning of these four syllables.
This is for the purpose of accomplishing the phrase of one's own perfect enlightenment.
Then, contemplating the bodhicitta,
one binds the aforementioned samaya-mudrā.
Then, having performed the preceding rites of generating the dharmadhātu, turning the wheel of Dharma, and the sword and seal mudrās,
empower the five locations of one's own body while reciting the respective root mantras for each.
Having prostrated to the Buddha, made vows, and dedicated the merit, he emerged from the dharma-hall.
He constantly turned the Mahāyāna teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and others,
and practiced walking meditation while sealing Buddha-seals upon stupas and scriptures.

One scroll of the Ritual for the Yoga Practice and Contemplation of the Heart Mantra of the Holy Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, [which states that] circumambulating a stūpa causes [the practice] to be swiftly accomplished.
